items.title: Ron Carter interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999

ctx.x: How did your professors feel about that? Or wasn’t it even an issue for them?

Well most of them didn’t really care. I went to class on time and did the homework. Some of them didn’t care for that kind of music so they didn’t like what I did in classes, and the school did not encourage a jazz profile. And the strange thing is at that time there was the Eastman Theater, there was a show called “Jazz for Moderns” that would travel throughout the country. And they played at the Eastman Theater, it was a wonderful auditorium, it seated maybe 2,000 people. And they had great bands going all…
force in music, it’s hard to understand how a classical institution would continue to ignore its presence.

items.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I had known Kenny from playing two dates with him, with Dizzy and Yusef.

ctx.x: Well, when I wanted to be a bandleader, I just wanted to be in front of the band physically. My feeling was that if you walk into the room with a trio – piano, bass and drums – people automatically assume this is a piano player's trio. And that's what that is, you know. But I wanted an instrument that would put me in front of the band, and so I put a bass player in the band. So the choices were either stand in front of the band physically, way out here in front of the band, or have the band here and help me…

I've always loved Ben Riley's playing and I thought Buster was the kind of guy who would be able to accompany a bass player and not be bent out of shape because his musicality is so high. Buster's a great sideman, by the way. So, I said, "Well, let me get a band together," and I had known Kenny from playing two dates with him, with Dizzy and Yusef. Occasionally, Miles would work opposite those bands and we'd be a block away and I'd get a chance to hear them. Then there was late Brother Bill, the saxophone player.…
